abstract: 'The purpose of this article is to study the problem of finding sharp lower bounds for the norm of the product of polynomials in the ultraproducts of Banach spaces $(X_i)_{\mathfrak U}$. We show that, under certain hypotheses, there is a strong relation between this problem and the same problem for the spaces $X_i$.'
address: 'IMAS-CONICET'
author:
- Jorge Tomás Rodríguez
title: On the norm of products of polynomials on ultraproducts of Banach spaces
---

Introduction
============

In this article we study the factor problem in the context of ultraproducts of Banach spaces. This problem can be stated as follows: for a Banach space $X$ over a field ${\mathbb K}$ (with ${\mathbb K}={\mathbb R}$ or ${\mathbb K}={\mathbb C}$) and natural numbers $k_1,\cdots, k_n$ find the optimal constant $M$ such that, given any set of continuous scalar polynomials $P_1,\cdots,P_n:X\rightarrow {\mathbb K}$, of degrees $k_1,\cdots,k_n$; the inequality $$\label{problema}
M \Vert P_1 \cdots P_n\Vert \ge  \, \Vert P_1 \Vert \cdots \Vert P_n \Vert$$ holds, where $\Vert P \Vert = \sup_{\Vert x \Vert_X=1} \vert P(x)\vert$. We also study a variant of the problem in which we require the polynomials to be homogeneous.

Recall that a function $P:X\rightarrow {\mathbb K}$ is a continuous $k-$homogeneous polynomial if there is a continuous $k-$linear function $T:X^k\rightarrow {\mathbb K}$ for which $P(x)=T(x,\cdots,x)$. A function $Q:X\rightarrow {\mathbb K}$ is a continuous polynomial of degree $k$ if $Q=\sum_{l=0}^k Q_l$ with $Q_0$ a constant, $Q_l$ ($1\leq l \leq k$) an $l-$homogeneous polynomial and $Q_k \neq 0$ .

The factor problem has been studied by several authors. In [@BST], C. Benítez,

Q:

MySQL replication: "Houston, We've Got a Problem"

I ran into a problem with our replication server. Essentially, we have 2 databases (database1 and database2). Master server has both. Slave has only database1. There is a
Replicate_Do_DB: database1

set in CHANGE MASTER TO configuration.
Now what happened is - we are using code igniter, and one of the programers created database2 and started inserting info into it. Code igniter sets a default database to database1. Now the result is for every query he produced - I get an error on SHOW SLAVE STATUS\G:
Error 'Table 'database2.tbl40' doesn't exist' on query. Default database: 'database1'. Query: 'INSERT INTO `database2`.`tbl40` (`date`, `day`) VALUES ('2011-04-26', '2011-04-26')'

So essentially, I he fixed the problem afterwards, but the replication doesn't work as there is around 1000 queries that will produce that error for replication server.
My question is - is there some way to clear queries like that from the binlog?
Or I need to write a script that will do a 
SET GLOBAL SQL_SLAVE_SKIP_COUNTER = 1;

for every query that produces and error ?

A:

If you really don't care about that table, you can use pt-slave-restart on the slave and have it skip those problems.  I would be conservative about running it and make sure that you are only skipping queries for the table/database that you don't care about or at least for only a specific error.
You didn't post what the error code was in the output from SHOW SLAVE STATUS, but I suspect it is error 1146.
For example, this will skip all errors for 1146:
pt-slave-restart -u root -p pass --error-numbers 1146

Or, you could try skipping all errors that reference that table
pt-slave-restart -u root -p pass --error-text 'database2'

Another way to do this would be to set replicate-ignore-db=database2 and restart MySQL on the slave, but there are some caveats to how that works that you should read about in the documentation

By the middle of the decade the question had stopped being academic. Three circuits had already split on whether a seller who merely facilitated a transaction could be treated as a manufacturer for purposes of the statute, and the practical consequences of the split were large enough that insurers had begun writing exclusions into policies in anticipation of the answer. The panel that finally took the issue en banc was, by its own account, uneasy about the invitation. It had declined two earlier petitions presenting the same question, and the order granting the third gave no reasons at all, which the bar read as a sign that the judges themselves did not yet agree on how the argument should be framed.

The panel began with the text. It noted that the operative phrase had been carried forward without amendment since the Reconstruction era, and that nearly every court to have construed it in the interim had read the governing verb narrowly. Where Congress had meant to reach the conduct alleged here, the panel said, it had used a different formulation in adjacent sections, and the difference could not be dismissed as stylistic. The court cited, among others, Camden County Board of Chosen Freeholders v. Beretta U.S.A. Corp., 273 F.3d 536, 540 (3d Cir. 2001), and Read v. Town of Mount Hope, 412 F. Supp. 2d 288, 295 (S.D.N.Y. 2005), for the proposition that a defendant must have exercised actual control over the instrumentality before liability will attach. Neither decision, the panel conceded, was strictly binding, but the reasoning of both had been followed widely enough that departing from it would require more than a plausible alternative reading.

The dissenting judges would have gone the other way. Their objection was not so much to the panel's reading of the words as to its confidence that the words still carried the meaning they had when they were written. Language drifts, the dissent observed, and a term of art that once described a narrow class of merchants may, after a century of use, describe a much wider one. The majority's approach, on this view, treated the dictionary as a constitution and left the statute fixed at the moment of enactment while the world around it changed.

The panel answered that the argument proved too much. If the meaning of every inherited phrase were permitted to drift with the usage of the day, no commercial statute would survive a generation, and the reliance interests that such statutes create would be impossible to protect. The legislature is free to amend when it wishes, and it has done so many times in neighbouring provisions without touching this one. Silence of that kind, sustained across repeated revisions of the surrounding text, is ordinarily taken as acquiescence in the settled reading, and the panel saw no reason to treat this instance differently.

It is true that the statute's remedial purpose counsels against a construction so tight that its protections become illusory. But purpose, the panel said, is a guide for resolving genuine ambiguity, not a licence to rewrite a provision that the legislature has left untouched. The dissent's parade of horribles, that manufacturers will escape liability by interposing a shell entity between themselves and the point of sale, was met with the observation that the plaintiffs in this very case had sued the upstream manufacturer directly, and had needed to plead nothing more than the relationship and the control it implied. The judgment of the district court was affirmed, and the mandate issued in due course.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The move began badly and got worse in the ordinary way. We had booked a van for eight in the morning, but the rental office on the ring road did not open until nine, and by the time the keys were in my hand the morning traffic had already filled the slip road with cars that would not let anything larger than a bicycle merge. The flat we were leaving was on the fourth floor of a building whose lift had been out of service since the spring, so every box came down the stairwell two at a time, passed hand to hand between the four of us, and stacked in a loading bay where rain had been getting in through a broken pane for what looked like years.

We counted 63 boxes at the end, plus a rolled rug, a broken chair, and a lamp that nobody wanted but nobody would throw away either. The van was rated for 14 cubic metres, which sounded generous until the sofa went in sideways and took up a third of the space. Between the four of us we had perhaps six hours before the van had to be back, and the drive across town was 212 kilometres of motorway and then a long stretch of single carriageway where the roadworks had been going on since the previous winter and where a temporary limit of 50 applied for most of the way.

We stopped once for fuel, at a service station where the price board said 349.9 and the coffee machine accepted cards but not the card I had. Two of the movers had sandwiches in a cool bag; the rest of us had crisps and a packet of biscuits that had been in the glovebox since the last trip. The satnav took us off the motorway one junction too early, so we spent 25 minutes threading through a village with a bridge too low for the van, reversing in a pub car park to the amusement of the lunchtime drinkers.

The new place was easier in every respect except the stairs. There were 18 steps to the first landing and another 14 to the second, and the boxes that had come down two at a time went up one at a time, which is the arithmetic of moving houses and nobody has ever found a way around it. By four in the afternoon the kitchen was in, the beds were assembled, and the kettle had been found in the box marked fragile, which is where nobody had thought to look. The neighbour on the ground floor knocked to say that the water from our washing machine had been running down his wall since lunchtime, and that he had put a bucket under it and would appreciate a plumber before the weekend.

What remains is the sorting: 11 bags of paper for recycling, a drawer of cables that fit nothing we still own, and a box of photographs, which we sat on the floor and went through until it was dark. The van went back at half past seven with 40 minutes to spare, and the man at the rental office said we were the third family that day to bring it back with the fuel light on.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long narrative in which every numeral is a plain quantity (63 boxes, 14 cubic metres, 212 kilometres), testing that the pole does not fire on digits in ordinary long prose where no label points at a reference value.

explanation_scores.explanation: The pole fires retrospectively on the digit token that opens a numeral inside a terse reference or notation run: the page/volume/docket/year/index value that a label, abbreviation or bracket points to ('477 F.2d 598', 'pp 143-167', 'No. 12-3842', '16-1 BCA 36,569 at 178,110', '1916: 139', 'October 25, 2004', 'January 17, 2018', 'DocReq 001013b', '[@Rempe2015a', 'for (i in 1:ncol(pval))'), peaking on the first one or two digits of that numeral and decaying over its remaining digits ('598' -> 0.97/0.81/0.25, '1040' -> 0.96/0.89/0.58/0.02). It stays near the floor on the same numerals embedded in ordinary words ('477 days, 598 pages' 0.35 vs 0.97 in the reporter slot), on spelled-out numbers, and in plain prose, while code label/value boundaries (' => $', ' =', ' public') form a weaker secondary family that the numeral reading does not cover.
